ch.s: This chapter covers: A plague of locusts (vv. 1–7); All sorts of people are called to lament it (vv. 8–13); They are to look to God (vv. 14–20). People named: Joel, Pethuel.
ch.mh: The most aged could not remember such calamities as were about to take place.
q: Read verses 1–7 (A plague of locusts). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 8–13 (All sorts of people are called to lament it), what do you learn about sacrifice and atonement?
Verse 4 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Joel 2:25. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Joel’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of family and generations in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Joel?

ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: Exhortations to fasting and prayer; blessings promised.
A promise of the Holy Spirit, and of future mercies.
bg: Joel was probably a resident in Judah, as his commission was to that people. He makes frequent mention of Judah and Jerusalem (1:14; 2:1, 15, 32; 3:1, 12, 17, 20, 21).

When David took it from the Jebusites (Josh. 15:63; 2 Sam. 5:7) he built on it a citadel and a palace, and it became "the city of David" (1 Kings 8:1; 2 Kings 19:21, 31; 1 Chr. 11:5). In the later books of the Old Testament this name was sometimes used (Ps. 87:2; 149:2; Isa. 33:14; Joel 2:1) to denote Jerusalem in general, and sometimes God's chosen Israel (Ps. 51:18; 87:5).
ch.s: This chapter covers: God's judgments (vv. 1–14); Exhortations to fasting and prayer; blessings promised (vv. 15–27); A promise of the Holy Spirit, and of future mercies (vv. 28–32). Places: Zion, Eden, Jerusalem.
ch.mh: The priests were to alarm the people with the near approach of the Divine judgments.
q: Read verses 1–14 (God's judgments). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 15–27 (Exhortations to fasting and prayer; blessings promised), what do you learn about war and conflict?
Verse 28 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Acts 2:16–21. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
Where do you see the theme of sacrifice and atonement in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Joel?
What is one specific way you can put this chapter into practice this week?
ch.aq: Our business therefore on earth must especially be, to secure an interest in our Lord Jesus Christ; and we should seek to be weaned from objects which will soon be torn from all who now make idols of them.
ch.a: Ask God to search your heart, confess what He shows you, and make any right amends.

o: God's judgments in the latter days.
The blessings the church shall enjoy.
bg: Joel was probably a resident in Judah, as his commission was to that people. He makes frequent mention of Judah and Jerusalem (1:14; 2:1, 15, 32; 3:1, 12, 17, 20, 21).

When David took it from the Jebusites (Josh. 15:63; 2 Sam. 5:7) he built on it a citadel and a palace, and it became "the city of David" (1 Kings 8:1; 2 Kings 19:21, 31; 1 Chr. 11:5). In the later books of the Old Testament this name was sometimes used (Ps. 87:2; 149:2; Isa. 33:14; Joel 2:1) to denote Jerusalem in general, and sometimes God's chosen Israel (Ps. 51:18; 87:5).
A fishery, a town on the Mediterranean coast, about 25 miles north of Tyre. It received its name from the "first-born" of Canaan, the grandson of Noah (Gen. 10:15, 19).
ch.s: This chapter covers: God's judgments in the latter days (vv. 1–8); The extent of these judgments (vv. 9–17); The blessings the church shall enjoy (vv. 18–21). People named: Jehoshaphat, Zidon, Sabeans. Places: Judah, Jerusalem, Zion, Tyre, Palestine.
ch.mh: The restoration of the Jews, and the final victory of true religion over all opposers, appear to be here foretold.
q: Read verses 1–8 (God's judgments in the latter days). What is happening, and what stands out to you most?
In verses 9–17 (The extent of these judgments), what do you learn about hope and restoration?
Verse 18 is one of the most cross-referenced verses in this chapter. Read it alongside Isaiah 35:6. How do the two passages shed light on each other?
What does Jehoshaphat’s part in this chapter teach you — as an example to follow or a warning to heed?
Where do you see the theme of war and conflict in this chapter, and how does it connect to the rest of Joel?
